Safe and Policy-Compliant Multi-Agent Orchestration
for Enterprise AI

1st Vinil Pasupuleti Affiliation: International Business Machines (IBM)
South Carolina, United States
IEEE Senior Member    2nd Shyalendar Reddy Allala Affiliation: Global Atlantic Financial
Indiana, United States
Independent Researcher Affiliation:     3rd Siva Rama Krishna Varma Bayyavarapu Affiliation: Docusign
Indiana, United States
IEEE Senior Member    4th Shrey Tyagi Affiliation: Salesforce Inc
North Carolina, United States
Independent Researcher
Abstract

Enterprise AI systems increasingly deploy multiple intelligent agents across mission-critical workflows that must satisfy hard policy constraints, bounded risk exposure, and comprehensive auditability (SOX, HIPAA, GDPR). Existing coordination methods—cooperative MARL, consensus protocols, and centralized planners—optimize expected reward while treating constraints implicitly. This paper introduces CAMCO (Constraint-Aware Multi-Agent Cognitive Orchestration), a runtime coordination layer that models multi-agent decision-making as a constrained optimization problem. CAMCO integrates three mechanisms: (i) a constraint projection engine enforcing policy-feasible actions via convex projection, (ii) adaptive risk-weighted Lagrangian utility shaping, and (iii) an iterative negotiation protocol with provably bounded convergence. Unlike training-time constrained RL, CAMCO operates as deployment-time middleware compatible with any agent architecture, with policy predicates designed for direct integration with production engines such as OPA. Evaluation across three enterprise scenarios—including comparison against a constrained Lagrangian MARL baseline—demonstrates zero policy violations, risk exposure below threshold (mean ratio 0.710.71), 92–97% utility retention, and mean convergence in 2.4 iterations.

Index Terms: 
Enterprise AI, multi-agent systems, safe reinforcement learning, constrained MDP, risk-aware optimization, orchestration, governance-ready AI, policy compliance

I Introduction

Enterprise AI-native architectures increasingly deploy multiple intelligent agents—LLM-based assistants [7], RL policies, and rule-augmented planners—across financial approval, payroll compliance, and cloud orchestration workflows [1, 16]. These settings impose hard policy constraints (approval chains, segregation of duties), bounded risk exposure, RBAC-gated execution feasibility, and auditability mandated by SOX, HIPAA, and GDPR [14].

Existing approaches address constraints during training (Safe RL, CMDPs [2, 3]) or via prompt-based guardrails that lack formal guarantees [15]. Enterprise deployments require a runtime coordination layer that enforces hard policy feasibility, regulates aggregate risk dynamically, and supports negotiated convergence—capabilities not provided by current frameworks. CAMCO fills this gap as lightweight deployment-time middleware compatible with any agent architecture.

Contributions.

  • •

    A formal enterprise multi-agent constrained decision model jointly capturing policy feasibility, execution feasibility, and bounded aggregate risk (Section III).

  • •

    CAMCO, a constraint-aware coordination algorithm with convex constraint projection and adaptive risk-weighted Lagrangian negotiation with provably bounded convergence (Section V).

  • •

    An architectural blueprint and evaluation demonstrating zero-violation coordination with 92–97% utility retention across three scenarios and four baselines (Sections IV, VI).

II Related Work

MARL methods (QMIX [10], MAPPO [11]) [1, 5, 6] use shaped rewards rather than hard runtime constraints. CMDPs [2], Safe RL [3], and CPO [4] formalize constraints during training; negotiation protocols [12, 13] ensure agreement without utility optimization. LLM-based agents [7, 8] and frameworks like AutoGen [9] lack formal constraint enforcement. Rule engines (OPA [20]) and governance frameworks [14, 15] enforce policy but lack optimization. Runtime verification [21] monitors specifications without multi-agent utility optimization. CAMCO uniquely combines utility optimization, hard policy feasibility, bounded risk, and negotiation at runtime.

Positioning. Table I summarizes how CAMCO compares to common alternatives across key enterprise requirements.

III Problem Formulation

III-A Enterprise Multi-Agent Decision Model

Let G={g1,…,gn}G=\{g_{1},\dots,g_{n}\} be a set of nn enterprise AI agents. At enterprise state s∈𝒮s\in\mathcal{S}, each agent gig_{i} proposes an action ai∈𝒜ia_{i}\in\mathcal{A}_{i}. Let Ui​(s,ai):𝒮×𝒜i→ℝ≥0U_{i}(s,a_{i}):\mathcal{S}\times\mathcal{A}_{i}\to\mathbb{R}_{\geq 0} denote the utility function of agent gig_{i}, and let ℛi​(ai):𝒜i→ℝ≥0\mathcal{R}_{i}(a_{i}):\mathcal{A}_{i}\to\mathbb{R}_{\geq 0} denote its risk contribution. Let τ>0\tau>0 denote an enterprise-configured aggregate risk threshold.

We seek a joint action vector 𝐚=(a1,…,an)\mathbf{a}=(a_{1},\dots,a_{n}) that maximizes aggregate utility subject to three classes of enterprise constraints:

max𝐚\displaystyle\max_{\mathbf{a}}\quad ∑i=1nUi​(s,ai)\displaystyle\sum_{i=1}^{n}U_{i}(s,a_{i}) (1)
s.t. Φ⁡(𝐚)=1\displaystyle\Phi(\mathbf{a})=1 (2)
∑i=1nℛi​(ai)≤τ\displaystyle\sum_{i=1}^{n}\mathcal{R}_{i}(a_{i})\leq\tau (3)
ai∈ℱi​(s),∀i∈{1,…,n}\displaystyle a_{i}\in\mathcal{F}_{i}(s),\ \forall i\in\{1,\dots,n\} (4)

III-B Constraint Definitions

Policy Feasibility Function Φ:𝒜1×⋯×𝒜n→{0,1}\Phi:\mathcal{A}_{1}\times\cdots\times\mathcal{A}_{n}\to\{0,1\} encodes joint policy validity, capturing approval chains, segregation of duties, and temporal ordering. Formally, Φ\Phi evaluates a conjunction of policy predicates {ϕk}k=1K\{\phi_{k}\}_{k=1}^{K}:

Φ(𝐚)=∏k=1Kϕk(𝐚),ϕk:𝒜1×⋯×𝒜n→{0,1}\Phi(\mathbf{a})=\prod_{k=1}^{K}\phi_{k}(\mathbf{a}),\quad\phi_{k}:\mathcal{A}_{1}\times\cdots\times\mathcal{A}_{n}\to\{0,1\} (5)

Execution Feasibility ℱi​(s)⊆𝒜i\mathcal{F}_{i}(s)\subseteq\mathcal{A}_{i} encodes the set of actions available to agent gig_{i} given current system state ss, incorporating RBAC permissions, resource availability, and temporal constraints:

ℱi​(s)={a∈𝒜i:perm​(gi,a,s)∧avail​(a,s)∧window​(a,s)}\mathcal{F}_{i}(s)=\{a\in\mathcal{A}_{i}:\text{perm}(g_{i},a,s)\wedge\text{avail}(a,s)\wedge\text{window}(a,s)\} (6)

Risk Model. Enterprise risk is nonlinear, state-dependent, and correlated across agents: ℛ⁡(𝐚,s)=f⁡(ℛ1​(a1,s),…,ℛn​(an,s))\mathcal{R}(\mathbf{a},s)=f\bigl(\mathcal{R}_{1}(a_{1},s),\dots,\mathcal{R}_{n}(a_{n},s)\bigr) where ff captures cross-agent interactions. For tractability, we adopt a weighted-additive decomposition:

ℛi​(ai)=∑d∈𝒟wd⋅ri,d​(ai)\mathcal{R}_{i}(a_{i})=\sum_{d\in\mathcal{D}}w_{d}\cdot r_{i,d}(a_{i}) (7)

where 𝒟\mathcal{D} denotes risk dimensions (financial, compliance, operational, reputational) with organization-configured weights wdw_{d}.

III-C Convergence Requirements

A coordination algorithm must satisfy: (1) Feasibility guarantee: the returned 𝐚∗\mathbf{a}^{*} satisfies Eqs. (2)–(4), or the algorithm fails to safe fallback; (2) Bounded runtime: termination within KmaxK_{\max} iterations; (3) Monotonic risk reduction: Rtot(k+1)≤Rtot(k)R_{\text{tot}}^{(k+1)}\leq R_{\text{tot}}^{(k)} when Rtot(k)>τR_{\text{tot}}^{(k)}>\tau.

IV CAMCO: Framework and Architecture

IV-A High-Level Architecture

Figure 1 illustrates how CAMCO integrates within an AI-native enterprise stack via a perceive–reason–coordinate–execute–reflect cycle.

IV-B Core Components

CAMCO’s coordination layer comprises three components: the Constraint Projection Engine (CPE), the Risk-Weighted Utility Engine (RWUE), and the Negotiation Loop.

The CPE projects each agent’s proposed action onto the nearest policy-compliant alternative. Given a proposed action aia_{i}, the CPE solves: ai′=arg⁡mina∈ℱi​(s)​‖a−ai‖a_{i}^{\prime}=\arg\min_{a\in\mathcal{F}_{i}(s)}\|a-a_{i}\| subject to all active policy predicates {ϕk}\{\phi_{k}\}, ensuring the corrected action remains close to the agent’s original intent while satisfying all hard constraints.

The RWUE computes adjusted utilities that internalize risk: U~i=Ui​(s,ai′)−λ⋅ℛi​(ai′)\tilde{U}_{i}=U_{i}(s,a_{i}^{\prime})-\lambda\cdot\mathcal{R}_{i}(a_{i}^{\prime}), where λ≥0\lambda\geq 0 is a Lagrangian multiplier updated each round via dual-ascent: λ(k+1)=λ(k)+α​(Rtot(k)−τ)+\lambda^{(k+1)}=\lambda^{(k)}+\alpha(R_{\text{tot}}^{(k)}-\tau)^{+}.

The Negotiation Loop orchestrates iterative re-proposals when joint actions fail risk or policy checks, tightening λ\lambda each round until RtotR_{\text{tot}} falls below τ\tau or KmaxK_{\max} is reached. If convergence fails, a safe fallback policy reverts all agents to their last known compliant configuration, guaranteeing no high-risk action set executes in production. This design draws on fail-safe principles from industrial control systems, where a well-defined safe state must always be reachable within bounded time. Formally, the fallback operator ℱ\mathcal{F} satisfies Φ⁡(ℱ⁡(𝐚))=1\Phi(\mathcal{F}(\mathbf{a}))=1 and ℛ⁡(ℱ⁡(𝐚),s)≤τ\mathcal{R}(\mathcal{F}(\mathbf{a}),s)\leq\tau for all states ss, providing a constructive proof that the orchestration never deadlocks in a non-compliant configuration.

(1) Constraint Projection Engine (CPE). The CPE transforms each agent proposal aia_{i} into a policy-feasible action ai′=Π𝒞​(ai)a_{i}^{\prime}=\Pi_{\mathcal{C}}(a_{i}) by solving a nearest-feasible-point problem over 𝒞i(s)=ℱi(s)∩{a:ϕk(⋅)=1,∀k}\mathcal{C}_{i}(s)=\mathcal{F}_{i}(s)\cap\{a:\phi_{k}(\cdot)=1,\forall k\}. For convex continuous action spaces, Π𝒞\Pi_{\mathcal{C}} is the standard Euclidean projection; for discrete enterprise actions, it is a constraint-satisfaction search with minimum edit distance. The projection satisfies idempotency (Π𝒞​(Π𝒞​(a))=Π𝒞​(a)\Pi_{\mathcal{C}}(\Pi_{\mathcal{C}}(a))=\Pi_{\mathcal{C}}(a)), guaranteed feasibility, and proximity (nearest feasible point). Figure 2 illustrates the projection process.

(2) Risk-Weighted Utility Engine (RWUE). The RWUE dynamically adjusts each agent’s utility with a Lagrangian risk penalty:

U~i​(s,ai,λ)=Ui​(s,ai)−λ⋅ℛi​(ai)\tilde{U}_{i}(s,a_{i};\lambda)=U_{i}(s,a_{i})-\lambda\cdot\mathcal{R}_{i}(a_{i}) (8)

The multiplier λ\lambda increases monotonically when aggregate risk exceeds τ\tau, ensuring monotonic risk reduction. Concretely, the update rule λ(t+1)=λ(t)+η⋅max⁡(0,Rtot(t)−τ)\lambda^{(t+1)}=\lambda^{(t)}+\eta\cdot\max(0,R_{\text{tot}}^{(t)}-\tau) follows a subgradient ascent on the dual variable, where the step size η\eta controls the trade-off between convergence speed and oscillation. In practice, CAMCO uses a diminishing step size ηt=η0/t\eta_{t}=\eta_{0}/\sqrt{t} to guarantee convergence to the saddle point of the Lagrangian while permitting aggressive early tightening. This approach is closely related to classical Lagrangian relaxation in constrained optimization [22], adapted here for the multi-agent, multi-constraint setting where each agent’s risk contribution is aggregated before the dual update.

The risk model ℛi​(ai)\mathcal{R}_{i}(a_{i}) combines domain-specific indicators whose weights are configured per deployment, decoupling risk semantics from optimization. In practice, convergence occurs within 2–4 rounds; KmaxK_{\max} is reached in only ∼\sim3% of proposals.

Lagrangian dual decomposition was chosen for: (i) privacy—agents report only projected actions [23]; (ii) continuous trade-off—quantitative utility–risk balance; (iii) auditability—λ\lambda acts as a shadow price of risk, transparent to regulators. The pipeline terminates in at most KmaxK_{\max} rounds (Theorem 1): monotonic increase of λ\lambda shrinks each agent’s rational action set until convergence or fallback.

(3) Negotiation Loop. The negotiation loop implements an iterative propose–project–evaluate cycle: each agent proposes an action maximizing U~i\tilde{U}_{i}, the CPE projects it, aggregate risk is evaluated, and if Φ⁡(𝐚′)=1\Phi(\mathbf{a}^{\prime})=1 and Rtot≤τR_{\text{tot}}\leq\tau the joint action is accepted; otherwise λ\lambda increases and agents re-propose. Figure 3 visualizes this protocol.

V-B Convergence Analysis

Theorem 1 (Bounded Convergence).

If each agent’s risk-shaped utility U~i​(s,⋅,λ)\tilde{U}_{i}(s,\cdot;\lambda) is continuous in λ\lambda and each ℛi\mathcal{R}_{i} is bounded above by r¯i<∞\bar{r}_{i}<\infty, then CAMCO either finds a feasible joint action or returns fail within KmaxK_{\max} iterations.

Proof sketch.

At each iteration where Rtot>τR_{\text{tot}}>\tau, λ\lambda increases by at least δ>0\delta>0. As λ→∞\lambda\to\infty, the risk-shaped utility makes any positive-risk action arbitrarily undesirable. Since each agent has at least one zero-risk safe default, agents eventually propose minimum-risk actions. If ∑iminai∈ℱi​(s)⁡ℛi​(ai)≤τ\sum_{i}\min_{a_{i}\in\mathcal{F}_{i}(s)}\mathcal{R}_{i}(a_{i})\leq\tau, convergence is guaranteed; otherwise fail is returned. The process terminates at KmaxK_{\max} regardless. ∎∎

Proposition 1 (Monotonic Risk Reduction).

Under CAMCO, if agents respond monotonically to λ\lambda (higher λ\lambda leads to weakly lower-risk proposals), then Rtot(k+1)≤Rtot(k)R_{\text{tot}}^{(k+1)}\leq R_{\text{tot}}^{(k)} for all kk where Rtot(k)>τR_{\text{tot}}^{(k)}>\tau.

VI Evaluation

VI-A Simulation Scenarios

We evaluate CAMCO using three enterprise-inspired simulation scenarios, each instantiating the constrained decision model from Section III:

  • •

    S1: Financial Approval Workflow. n=4n=4 agents (requester, manager, compliance officer, CFO) coordinating multi-stage payment approvals with escalation rules, amount-based thresholds, and segregation-of-duties constraints. Risk model: financial exposure weighted by transaction amount and counterparty rating.

  • •

    S2: Payroll Adjustment Task. n=3n=3 agents (HR analyst, payroll processor, audit reviewer) handling salary adjustments with compliance checks, executive compensation sensitivity thresholds, and retroactive adjustment limits. Risk model: compliance violation probability and audit exposure.

  • •

    S3: Hybrid Cloud Deployment. n=5n=5 agents (developer, DevOps, security reviewer, change manager, SRE) managing production deployments with RBAC-gated permissions, data sovereignty constraints, change window restrictions, and rollback readiness. Risk model: service disruption probability and RTO deviation.

Each scenario is run for 500 episodes with randomized initial states.

VI-B Baselines

  1. 1.

    B1: Unconstrained MARL – agents maximize individual reward without constraint enforcement (reward-first).

  2. 2.

    B2: Centralized greedy optimizer – single planner selects highest-utility joint action without risk bounding (utility-first heuristic).

  3. 3.

    B3: Static rule/workflow engine – evaluates policy constraints only, rejects non-compliant actions without optimization or negotiation (policy-only).

  4. 4.

    B4: Lagrangian MARL – each agent independently applies Lagrangian constraint handling (per-agent λ\lambda update) without joint constraint projection or multi-agent negotiation protocol (constrained-but-uncoordinated).

VI-C Metrics

Table II defines evaluation metrics aligned to enterprise concerns.

VI-D Results

Table III presents results across all scenarios and methods.

Key findings. CAMCO achieves zero policy violations across all scenarios, outperforming B1 (18–31%), B2 (5–13%), and B4 (4–9%). It eliminates B4’s residual violations caused by lack of joint feasibility projection. Risk exposure stays well below threshold (R¯/τ∈[0.68,0.74]\bar{R}/\tau\in[0.68,0.74]), utility retention reaches 92–97% (vs. B3’s 66–75%), deadlock rates remain below 2% (vs. B3’s 8–19%), and mean convergence occurs in 2.1–2.8 iterations. Sensitivity analysis confirms 100% compliance across τ∈[0.4,1.4]\tau\in[0.4,1.4], with utility degrading gracefully from 99% to 78% at tighter thresholds.

VI-E Limitations

CAMCO’s effectiveness depends on risk-model calibration quality; the linear-additive decomposition used here may underestimate compounding risk in highly correlated workflows, though extending to nonlinear risk functions is straightforward given the monotone-Lipschitz requirement. The projection operator’s efficiency relies on convexity for continuous spaces and moderate |𝒜i||\mathcal{A}_{i}| for discrete; scaling beyond |𝒜i|>103|\mathcal{A}_{i}|>10^{3} would require constraint-programming solvers.

VII Conclusion

This paper introduced CAMCO, a constraint-aware multi-agent cognitive orchestration framework for AI-native enterprise systems. By integrating convex constraint projection, adaptive risk-weighted Lagrangian utility shaping, and an iterative negotiation protocol with provably bounded convergence, CAMCO produces globally feasible joint actions that satisfy enterprise policy constraints and risk bounds while retaining 92–97% of unconstrained utility.

Our evaluation across three enterprise scenarios and four baselines—including constrained Lagrangian MARL—demonstrates that CAMCO eliminates policy violations entirely (vs. 4–31% for alternatives) while avoiding the excessive conservatism of pure rule-based approaches (which sacrifice 25–34% of utility and suffer 8–19% deadlock rates).

Future work includes adaptive risk calibration via Bayesian updating, hierarchical coordination for large-scale deployments (n>20n>20), and empirical validation with production policy engines (OPA, Cedar).
